title: From a convincing patch to a defensible decision
subtitle: A plain-English field guide to backward reasoning, semantic falsification, Git evidence and the point where computers must stop claiming success.
audience: Curious readers, engineering leads and CTOs

pages.title: A green build is not the same as a good decision
pages.deck: AI can produce code, tests and polished dashboards faster than a reviewer can reconstruct why they exist. The question is not whether a change looks plausible. It is: what would have to be true before someone should accept it?

blocks.text: Imagine a tiny issue-reporting web app. A visitor must file a problem, see it again after reloading the page, and be unable to close another person's report. A screenshot of a working form proves none of those three conditions by itself.
A six-stage journey: read the arrows as obligations, not magic

rows: Accept, reject or request more proof
blocks.caption: Figure 1  Method independent of any AI vendor. The diagram is an authored synthesis of CORA's existing source workflow [E01-E04].

blocks.text: Derive requirements backward, rather than writing a hopeful to-do list

Start at the desired final behavior, then ask what must hold for it to be true. For the issue app, success needs every one of these leaves: a POST creates a record; SQLite commits it; GET after reload returns it; roles forbid an outsider from closing it; invalid input is rejected; recovery and the human owner are known. This is an AND graph: five green leaves cannot compensate for one missing mandatory leaf.

rows: A visitor can safely file and recover a report
POST + durable storage + readback + authorization + negative tests
NOT_RUN / REFUTED / BLOCKED, not a synthetic PASS

blocks.text: An authorized coding tool may implement one reversible vertical slice, e.g., POST → SQLite → GET. A repository-assurance tool may inspect the resulting commits and receipts. Neither tool can grant a company's release permission. Next revision, re-check the same claims against the new HEAD. [E01-E03]
Key distinction: a plan says what should be observed; a source test says what was checked; a trusted runtime receipt says what happened there; an accountable person decides whether it is enough.

pages.kicker: A REAL TRACE  /  FROM SCREEN TO SYSTEM
pages.title: What a screenshot can tell you — and what it cannot
pages.deck: A marked-up screen is a useful observation. It is not yet an explanation of the cause. The method turns the visible symptom into testable hypotheses, then descends through the implementation.

blocks.text: In a public ICTC audit, an evidence register links 15 annotated screenshot references to 12 issue families and 28 individually owned findings (22 P3A; 6 P3B). Those counts belong to the source register, not to independently re-examined images: the original 15 image bytes were not present in the pinned public main tree checked for this guide. [E06-E07]
One bounded case: content that looked 'below' a header

The design intent said supporting procedure information belonged below the canonical header. The root-cause analysis found that the content was physically nested inside the header element even where copy and tests called it 'below'. This is a semantic-to-physical mismatch: words describe one relation, the browser DOM encodes another. [E07]

blocks.text: Why this must reach the 'metal'

A screenshot can suggest crowded buttons, hidden information or a misleading AI indicator. It cannot prove whether CSS is clipping a component, whether the DOM parent is wrong, whether a click reaches an authenticated HTTP endpoint, whether SQLite persists state, or whether a real mobile reader can complete the task. Each layer needs a different witness: annotated pixels → DOM/geometry → browser action → server/DB readback → real device/user. Escalate until the claim and the evidence refer to the same layer.

Counterexample: passing a source-only check cannot certify pixel-perfect layout or practical accessibility. The public ICTC model also runs one million synthetic cases; that is not one million independently captured screenshots. [E06-E10]

pages.title: Turn a claim into bytes, then try to break it
pages.deck: The words sound exotic; the operations are familiar engineering practices: make inputs reproducible, test a prediction against an independent rule, and stop only within a defined search boundary.

blocks.text: 1. 'Blob' means materialize an exact version, not prove it is true

Git stores file bytes as content-addressed blobs, directory mappings as trees, and revision history as commits. Pin BASE and HEAD; specify a target path, expected behavior, affected owners and consumer links; write a reversible patch and tests. If a blob changes, evidence tied to the old blob must be reconsidered. The hash identifies bytes — not an authentic reviewer, correct behavior or a trusted machine. [E01-E04]

rows: Report survives reload and unauthorized close is refused
file blob → tree → commit HEAD → named test log
owner + review + effective host policy, verified separately

blocks.text: 2. 'Falsify' means make the expected failure observable

Before testing, write an oracle independent of the patch: for example, 'a user without the closure role receives a denial and no database state changes'. Introduce an invalid role, an unknown evidence grade, stale source SHA or deliberately broken DOM parent in a disposable copy. Re-run the specific oracle and preserve the command, environment, expected result and outcome. KILLED = the oracle caught the injected fault; SURVIVED = it did not; INCONCLUSIVE = the run cannot decide. Never label an unexecuted test a pass. [E04]
3. 'Saturate' means bounded no-new-information, not universal correctness

Group faults by meaning, not merely by count: wrong owner; missing dependency; stale provenance; unauthorized state transition; broken source-to-runtime link; lost rollback. Generate seeded variants, including meaningful combinations. Keep an independent expected-result rule, record newly discovered material classes, then run a fresh tail. A tail with no new class supports only model-bounded saturation; a surviving unsafe case or a new class reopens the design. If new classes keep appearing, remodel the taxonomy instead of declaring victory. [E05]

blocks.caption: Figure 3  Deterministic finite testing: reproducibility and search coverage are not production proof. [E04-E05]

blocks.text: Scale carefully: 100 deliberately injected editorial/data faults in this document's own local campaign are not 100 independent real-world failures. CORA reports seeded 10-million-case modeled streams; ICTC also models one-million-case UI fault families. Neither number means that many physical source edits, browser runs or human tests. [E05,E10]

blocks.text: A scientific result worth keeping even when it is null

In PR73/MS-10, 11 purposively selected pull requests from five projects yielded 92 applicable evidence slots; 70 were unobserved in the collected dossier (not 70 proven defects). A typed decision rule and an equally informed strong checklist tied on 16/16 selected fixtures. Forty-four role-formatted briefings were generated, but no human participants were tested. Better decisions, comprehension, causation and total cost savings are not measured. [E11]
A CTO's falsifiable one-PR pilot

Choose one relevant change. Freeze its real BASE/HEAD and its risk. Give both CORA-guided review and a strong checklist the same evidence. Compare harmful false closures, missing-risk detection, time spent by engineers and reviewers, compute/CI cost, rework and rollback readiness. Require a real target oracle and an independent authorizer before expanding use. If the added assurance costs more without improving decisions at this risk level, reject the adoption hypothesis.

This standalone guide contains the method and the main counterexamples; the machine-readable pin ledger alongside the source records full Git blob SHA values. Screenshot originals, independent reader tests and external approvals are not claimed. Programme terminology: AOSP (Augmented Ontological-Semantic Platforms), ROA (Reticular Observer Architectures); neither is a prerequisite for using the method.
